editorial.description: The pink paper remains the single most-monitored title among the comms professionals Inkline is built for, and for a reason that has little to do with circulation: an FT story is what moves an IR phone line before the market opens. Lex and Alphaville carry disproportionate weight relative to their length, and Due Diligence frequently breaks M&A detail hours ahead of the wires. Feed access has quietly narrowed over the past few years, with several desk feeds no longer publicly listed, which is precisely the kind of gap hand-verification exists to close. If a client is listed in London, this is the first monitor to set up.

Ownership by trust rather than proprietor shapes this newsroom's behaviour in ways monitors learn to anticipate: investigations run long, follow-ups arrive in waves, and a story a client hopes has passed can resurface weeks later with new documents. Its feed provision is among the most generous of any British national, covering desks most rivals stopped syndicating years ago. For reputation work the Media desk deserves particular attention, as it is where coverage about coverage tends to start. The open-access model also means every link in a morning brief resolves for every reader, which matters more than it sounds.

Reach is the whole argument here. A story that makes the broadcaster's front page reaches an audience an order of magnitude beyond any national newspaper, so crisis teams treat its pickup as the threshold between a trade story and a public one. Less obvious to newcomers is how conservative the desk feeds are: syndicated output trails the website's live pages by several minutes during breaking news, which is worth knowing before promising anyone real-time alerts. Regional output is thinner in the feeds than on air, a gap Inkline flags rather than papers over.

Wire copy is upstream of everything else a monitor reads, which makes this agency's retreat from public syndication one of the more consequential quiet changes in the industry: the feeds most aggregators still list stopped updating when the website moved behind registration. Inkline resolves the desks through verified alternatives and says so plainly on the record for each. Speed remains the reason to monitor a wire at all, as corporate statements routinely appear here before the papers that will later analyse them. A headline here is a starting gun. The full story follows elsewhere, usually within the hour.

A weekly rhythm makes this title easy to monitor badly. The print edition lands Thursday evening London time, and that is when a fortnight of quiet can turn into the definitive framing of an issue, unsigned and therefore speaking with the full weight of the institution. Bylines are absent by policy, which changes how a mention should be escalated: there is no correspondent relationship to manage, only an editorial line. Daily digital pieces between editions have grown steadily and now justify continuous monitoring rather than a Thursday check.

For a London comms team the practical question is timing, and the answer is awkward: the heaviest publishing window opens as the UK working day ends, so a Journal story about a European client often breaks into an unstaffed evening. Building it into an automated evening brief solves what a manual check cannot. Heard on the Street occupies roughly the position Lex does at its London rival, brief and market-moving, and Opinion operates with a noticeably freer hand than the news desks. Feed coverage is stable but narrower than the site's full section map.

Anyone monitoring a DAX-listed client learns quickly that the German business conversation runs through Düsseldorf, not Frankfurt. Company coverage here regularly carries supervisory-board detail the international press picks up a day later, and often only partially. The weekday publishing pattern is pronounced, with output thinning sharply after Friday afternoon, so a weekend gap in mentions is normal rather than a monitoring fault. Inkline pairs it with on-device summarisation, which turns German-language desk output into something an English-speaking team can actually triage at speed.

The afternoon matters here in a way that trips up monitors calibrated to London or New York rhythms. This paper's heritage as an evening title survives in its publishing curve, which peaks after lunch Paris time, so a morning-only sweep of French coverage will consistently miss its lead stories. An English-language edition now runs in parallel and is worth adding for teams without French, though it carries a subset of the desks. Économie coverage of French-listed companies tends toward the analytical rather than the incremental, which makes it better for context than for alerts.

Journalists read this to find out what is happening to journalism, which makes it the closest thing the industry has to a staffing wire: editor moves, desk closures and title sales appear here first, and each one changes who a comms team should be pitching. The audience-data series has become a reference in its own right, tracking which publishers are actually growing rather than which claim to be. For anyone maintaining a media list by hand, this title is the maintenance schedule.

Account moves are the currency of this trade title, and its coverage of them doubles as a live map of who advises whom, which is intelligence in the plainest sense of the word. Agency league tables and the annual awards season generate predictable coverage spikes worth anticipating rather than discovering. Its analysis desk has sharpened noticeably on AI's effect on the profession, a beat with obvious relevance to anyone reading this directory. Monitoring it is less about client mentions than about watching the industry's plumbing.

Free at Tube stations and free online, which gives Square Mile stories a reach into general readership that its circulation figures understate. The desk moves fast on IPO and listings news and is often the first written coverage a mid-cap announcement receives. Since the ecommerce group's acquisition the opinion pages have grown livelier, and comms teams underrate them at their peril, because a sharp column here gets screenshotted into the City's group chats by mid-morning.

The New York Times is the largest newsroom in American journalism and the paper most likely to set the day's agenda across politics, world affairs and culture. Its investigations travel: a Times scoop is routinely the story every other publication spends the week matching. For monitoring purposes that makes it a leading indicator rather than just a record. Articles sit behind a meter, and the free allowance is modest, so treat headlines as the alert and budget clicks for what matters.

The Washington Post remains the essential read on the American federal government. Its reporting strength is proximity: the White House, Congress, the agencies and the security establishment are covered with a depth no outsider matches. Business and technology desks have grown sharply in recent years. A meter applies to articles. If your work touches US policy or regulation, the Post belongs in the monitor list even when the client is not American, because Washington decisions rarely stay domestic.

Bloomberg is the wire the markets actually move on. Speed and precision on companies, deals, central banks and commodities are the core product, funded by the terminal business rather than advertising, which shows in the discipline of the copy. The paywall is hard and the subscription is priced for professionals. For a comms team, Bloomberg headlines are often the first public signal that a story about your client has broken into the financial press.

The Associated Press is the news cooperative underneath much of what you read elsewhere; thousands of publications reprint its copy verbatim. Following AP directly means seeing the wire version of events before local rewrites add their angles, which is precisely what you want when tracking how a story spreads. Coverage is free to read, sober in register, and global in reach, with particular authority on US state-level news that national titles skip.

CNBC covers business as live events: markets, earnings, deals and the executives behind them, with the broadcast newsroom's instinct for the moment something changes. Its digital coverage is free to read and quick, making it a practical early-warning layer for anything with a share price attached. Interviews matter here; a chief executive's unguarded phrase on CNBC air frequently becomes the day's corporate story.

CNN is the American broadcaster with the largest international news operation, and its digital output reflects that reach: breaking news at pace, US politics in volume, and correspondents in places most outlets cover from a desk. Its digital coverage is free to read in full. In a monitoring stack it serves as the mass-audience barometer; when a corporate or policy story crosses onto CNN's front page, it has left the trade press and entered the public conversation.

Politico covers the machinery of politics: who is deciding what, which way the votes lean, and what the lobbying looks like from inside the room. The Brussels edition gives it unusual strength on European regulation as well as Washington. Core coverage is free, with the deepest material reserved for its professional subscriptions. Communications teams read it because policy risk usually surfaces here first, in the newsletters, before it becomes a mainstream headline.

Axios built its newsroom around brevity: short items, bolded takeaways, and a promise not to waste the reader's morning. That format makes it dense with signal for a monitoring workflow, since each item is effectively a pre-written summary. Coverage spans US politics, business, technology and local city editions, free to read. Its scoops tend to be small and early rather than long and definitive, which is exactly what a keyword catches best.

The Times of London carries an authority in British public life that outlasts news cycles: its reporting and its leader column are read in Westminster as a signal of where establishment opinion sits. Politics, law, business and sport are all covered with depth. The paywall is hard, with essentially nothing free beyond headlines. For UK reputation work it is one of the titles a story must be judged by, clicks budgeted accordingly.

The Telegraph is the house paper of the British centre-right, strongest on politics, business and its long tradition of foreign reporting. Its front page choices reliably indicate which stories will run inside the Conservative political world. A meter applies, with a small free allowance. Monitor it alongside The Guardian for the fastest read on how a UK story is polarising, since the two often frame the same facts in opposite directions.

Sky News is Britain's rolling news channel, and its digital operation carries the same virtue: speed. Breaking UK stories frequently appear here minutes before the newspaper sites, and its political journalists break stories of their own. The coverage costs nothing to read. In a monitoring stack Sky functions as the tripwire; the considered analysis arrives elsewhere later, but the first alert that something is happening in Britain very often carries this masthead.

Nikkei Asia is the English-language window into Asia's business press, produced by Japan's dominant financial news group. Corporate Japan, Chinese technology, supply chains and regional politics are covered with sourcing Western outlets rarely match. The paywall is hard. For any client with Asian operations, suppliers or competitors, it is the difference between reading about the region and reading from it.

Le Figaro is France's newspaper of the centre-right and one of its two agenda-setting dailies. National politics, business and culture are core strengths, and its opinion pages carry weight in French corporate and political life. A meter applies to articles. Paired with Le Monde, it gives a monitoring list stereo coverage of any French story, with the two papers' framings mapping the political spectrum between them.

El País is Spain's paper of record and the most-read Spanish-language newspaper in the world, with an edition serving Latin America that extends its reach far beyond Madrid. Politics, international affairs and culture are its traditional strengths. Articles are metered. For monitoring, its position matters: a Spanish or Latin American story that reaches El País has reached the region's boardrooms.

Der Spiegel is Germany's investigative institution, a weekly magazine whose newsroom breaks the stories German politics then spends months answering. Its digital edition publishes daily across politics, business and society. A meter applies, with the deepest investigations reserved for subscribers. If a German-speaking market matters to your work, Spiegel is the title whose interest in a subject you least want to discover late.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung speaks for and to the German establishment: precise, conservative in temperament, and unusually strong on economics, law and finance from the country's financial capital. Articles are metered. Its business pages are required reading for anyone whose clients touch German industry, and its judgements travel into Brussels policy debates with more weight than most national papers manage.

Süddeutsche Zeitung, published from Munich, is Germany's great liberal daily and one half of the duopoly, with the FAZ, that frames serious German debate. It has a strong investigative record, including its central role in the Panama Papers. A meter applies to articles, with investigations often held for subscribers. Monitoring German coverage without it means seeing only half the country's argument.

Neue Zürcher Zeitung is the Swiss German-language daily with a reputation for rigour that extends well beyond Switzerland; its economics and international coverage are read across the German-speaking world. Articles are metered. For financial services and commodities work, where Switzerland is never incidental, NZZ coverage is a signal worth treating separately from the German papers it superficially resembles.

Al Jazeera English covers the Middle East, Africa and South Asia with correspondent depth that Western newsrooms have largely retreated from, and its live coverage of unfolding crises in those regions is frequently the fullest available. All of it is free to read. Its state funding from Qatar is context worth holding; its field reporting remains indispensable for stories where it is often the only English-language outlet present.

The South China Morning Post is Hong Kong's English-language daily and the most-read English source on China. Its position is unique and delicate: close enough to report mainland business and politics with real sourcing, scrutinised precisely because of that closeness. A meter applies. For China-exposed clients it is essential, best read alongside a mainland-sceptical source for parallax.

The Globe and Mail is Canada's national newspaper, with its Report on Business section standing as the country's financial press of record. Ottawa politics, energy and mining are natural strengths given the economy it covers. A meter applies to articles. Any client with Canadian operations, listings or regulators should have it monitored; Canadian stories often stay in Canadian media longer than teams abroad expect.

The Sydney Morning Herald is one of Australia's two agenda-setting metropolitan dailies, strong on national politics, business and the investigations it shares across its newspaper group. A meter applies. Australian coverage runs on Sydney time, which for European teams means stories break overnight; a monitor here surfaces them with the morning brief rather than at the point a client calls.

The Times of India is the world's largest-circulation English-language newspaper and the broadest single window into Indian news. National politics, business and city coverage arrive at volume, free to read. The sheer output argues for following it through monitors and keywords rather than as a raw feed, letting the terms you care about surface from the flow.

NPR is American public radio's news organisation, and its written coverage carries the qualities of its broadcasting: measured, well sourced, and strong on explanation over heat. Politics, science and culture are particular strengths. Its journalism is free to read, as public media should be. In a monitoring stack it earns a place as a calibration source, useful for judging how a story reads when told without a proprietor's angle.

TechCrunch is the news desk of the startup economy: funding rounds, launches, shutdowns and the venture capital behind them. Coverage is free to read, fast, and unashamedly inside the industry it reports on. For communications work it matters twice over: once because clients raise money, and again because it is where technology-sector reputations are often first made and first tested.

The Verge covers consumer technology as an industry and a culture: products, platforms and the policy fights around them, written for readers who follow the sector closely. A meter applies to some of its work. Product-launch coverage here shapes wider reporting, and its reviews carry commercial consequence, which for technology clients makes it monitoring rather than optional reading.

Semafor is the newest name on this list, a digital newsroom built by senior editors from Bloomberg and BuzzFeed News around a format that separates reported fact from the reporter's view. Its Washington, business and Africa coverage have established themselves quickly, largely through newsletters. Free to read. Worth monitoring because its scoops increasingly seed the day's coverage elsewhere.
